title: LLP formation and members' duties
subtitle: Incorporating a limited liability partnership and what members owe each other
objectives: State how an LLP is incorporated and explain why its certificate of incorporation is conclusive evidence that the registration requirements were met
Explain the LLP's separate legal personality, members' liability limited to their agreed contribution, and the designated members' filing responsibilities under s 8
Explain why LLP members owe no automatic fiduciary duties to one another absent agreement, and identify where general principles can still impose one

leadingAuthorities.role: Sets the incorporation document requirements delivered to the Registrar
Certificate of incorporation as conclusive evidence of compliance with registration requirements
Designated members and their filing responsibilities
Default provisions governing members' mutual rights and duties absent an LLP agreement

leadingAuthorities.citation: F&C Alternative Investments (Holdings) Ltd v Barthelemy (No 2) [2011] EWCA Civ 1103
leadingAuthorities.role: Confirms fiduciary duties are not automatic on membership but can arise from the functions a member actually undertakes

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Trainees routinely assume an LLP is 'just a partnership with a company wrapper'. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this note appears: 'You know the structure — this lesson is about the two places clients get badly surprised: designated member liability for filings, and the absence of automatic duties.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on the LLP formation rules before. The test pool below leans on client scenarios — who is liable for what, and whether a duty exists absent agreement.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and be precise about what 'conclusive evidence' actually forecloses — the rest of the lesson assumes you can state the incorporation sequence without prompting.

overview.hook: Two accountants set up an LLP together, split the work informally for three years, then fall out. One accuses the other of putting personal interests ahead of the firm's. There's no LLP agreement — they never got round to it. Is that a breach of duty? The honest answer is: usually not, and that surprises almost everyone who has practised under a traditional partnership.

parts.heading: From incorporation document to conclusive certificate
parts.voice: structural — walks the registration sequence in order
body: An LLP does not exist until it is registered. Under s 2 of the Limited Liability Partnerships Act 2000 (LLPA 2000), an incorporation document is delivered to the Registrar of Companies, subscribed by at least two persons who are 'associated for carrying on a lawful business with a view to profit'. That phrase matters: an LLP cannot be formed for a non-profit purpose, and a single promoter cannot incorporate one alone — a traditional partnership needs two partners to exist at all, and an LLP inherits that starting point even though it is a body corporate.

The incorporation document must state the LLP's name, the address of its registered office, the names and addresses of the persons who are to be members on incorporation, and which of them are to be designated members (or a statement that all members are to be designated members).

Once the Registrar is satisfied the requirements are met, a certificate of incorporation is issued. Section 3 makes that certificate conclusive evidence that the registration requirements of the Act have been complied with and that the LLP is duly incorporated as an LLP on the date given. In practice this closes off almost any later challenge to the LLP's existence on a procedural defect — a solicitor cannot unpick a completed incorporation by pointing to a filing irregularity.

components.definition: A statutory device (LLPA 2000, s 3; mirrored for companies at CA 2006, s 15) that treats the certificate as settling the question of due incorporation once and for all — it cannot be reopened by evidence of a defect in the registration process.

interaction.prompt: A single sole practitioner tries to incorporate an LLP on her own, intending to bring in a second member later. Can she do this?
options: No — at least two persons associated for carrying on a lawful business with a view to profit must subscribe the incorporation document
Yes — an LLP, like a private company, can be formed with a single member from the outset
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. The LLP's partnership ancestry shows here: unlike a company, it needs two founding members before it can be incorporated at all.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite — check the wording of s 2 again. An LLP needs at least two persons associated for a lawful profit-making business to subscribe the incorporation document; a single promoter cannot do this alone.

parts.heading: Separate personality, and liability limited to what was agreed
parts.voice: comparative — sets the LLP against the traditional partnership it replaced for many firms
body: An LLP is a body corporate with legal personality separate from its members, and unlimited capacity (LLPA 2000, s 1(2)–(3)). It can hold property, sue and be sued, and enter contracts in its own name — none of which is true of a traditional partnership, which has no existence apart from the partners themselves.

That separate personality is what makes limited liability possible. A member's liability to contribute to the LLP's assets on a winding up is limited to whatever they have agreed to contribute — there is no equivalent of a general partner's unlimited personal exposure for the firm's debts. This is the central commercial reason firms of solicitors, accountants and architects moved from traditional partnerships to the LLP structure from 2001 onwards.

Two qualifications matter for practice. First, a member who has given a personal guarantee (commonly required by a bank lending to the LLP) remains liable on that guarantee regardless of the LLP's limited liability status — the statute protects members from the firm's debts, not from their own separate contractual promises. Second, members can still face personal liability in tort for their own negligent acts, subject to the usual rules on assumption of responsibility.

components.label: What separate legal personality actually changes
points: The LLP, not the members, owns the firm's property and is the contracting party
The LLP, not the members, is sued on the firm's contractual and tortious liabilities in the first instance
A member's exposure on a winding up is capped at their agreed contribution — unlike a general partner's unlimited liability
Personal guarantees and a member's own tortious liability survive the LLP wrapper — limited liability is not a shield against a member's own separate promises or negligence

interaction.prompt: Which of the following best captures what LLPA 2000, s 1 actually confers on an incorporated LLP?
options: Separate legal personality and unlimited capacity, as a body corporate distinct from its members
A tax status identical to a traditional partnership, with no change to legal personality
Limited liability for members but no separate legal personality for the firm itself
interaction.explanation: Section 1 does the structural work: it makes the LLP a body corporate with legal personality separate from its members. The limited liability consequence for members follows from that separate personality — it is not a standalone grant.

parts.heading: Designated members: the ones on the hook for filing
parts.voice: practical — the section a trainee actually has to apply on a file
body: Every LLP must have at least two designated members (s 8 LLPA 2000). If the incorporation document, or a later notice, does not specify who they are, every member is treated as a designated member by default — there is no gap in coverage.

Designated members carry the LLP's compliance workload: signing and filing the annual accounts, notifying the Registrar of changes to membership or to the registered office, appointing an auditor where required, and acting on the LLP's behalf if it is wound up. An ordinary (non-designated) member has no such statutory filing duty — but that does not mean they are passengers; it only means the filing obligation itself sits with the designated members.

This distinction catches trainees advising on management structure: being a designated member is not a seniority title and carries no extra share of profits by default — it is purely a compliance role created by statute. Firms sometimes rotate it; nothing in the Act says it must be permanent or tied to any particular status within the LLP.

components.factsShort: Every LLP needs at least two designated members, whether specified expressly or by default (all members become designated members if none are named).
components.ratioShort: Designated members are responsible for the LLP's statutory filings and compliance obligations; ordinary members have no equivalent statutory filing duty.

expanded.facts: An LLP's incorporation document may name certain members as designated members. If it names none, or if the number named falls below two, every person who is a member is by default a designated member under s 8(2).
expanded.judgmentExtract: Section 8(3)–(4) sets out the designated members' functions: signing accounts, delivering the confirmation statement and other filings to the Registrar, appointing an auditor, and acting for the LLP on a winding up.
expanded.significance: This is a compliance allocation, not a status or profit-share marker. Advising a client to name only trusted, engaged members as designated members is good practice, because those are the individuals exposed to the criminal offence of failing to file (mirroring company director default filing offences).

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that determines whether every member of this LLP is automatically a designated member.
interaction.scenarioText: An LLP's incorporation document lists four members but does not identify any of them as a designated member. The LLP has been trading for two years without ever filing a notice naming designated members.
tappableSpans: does not identify any of them as a designated member
interaction.correctSpan: does not identify any of them as a designated member
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Once the incorporation document (or any later notice) fails to name at least two designated members, s 8(2) treats every member as a designated member by default — there is no vacuum in who is responsible for filing.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at what triggers the default rule. It is the absence of a valid designation — not how long the LLP has traded — that brings s 8(2) into play.

parts.heading: Why members don't automatically owe each other fiduciary duties
parts.voice: argumentative — states the counter-intuitive rule, then qualifies it honestly
body: Here is the point that trips up anyone coming from a traditional partnership background: unlike partners under the Partnership Act 1890 (which imposes duties of good faith, full disclosure and no unauthorised profit as a matter of law), LLP members owe each other no automatic fiduciary duties purely by virtue of membership.

The mutual rights and duties of LLP members are, first and foremost, a matter of contract — set out in an LLP agreement if the members have made one. Where there is no agreement, or it is silent on a point, the LLP Regulations 2001 import a set of default provisions (modelled on Partnership Act 1890 rules, adapted for the LLP context) covering matters like profit-sharing, management participation and expulsion. But even these defaults do not recreate the full fiduciary regime a traditional partnership carries automatically.

That said, 'no automatic fiduciary duty from membership alone' is not the same as 'no fiduciary duty ever'. General principles of agency and equity can still impose a fiduciary duty on a member who, in substance, takes on a role involving discretion over the LLP's affairs or other members' interests — the duty then arises from that functional role, not from the bare fact of membership. This is a genuinely fact-sensitive area rather than a bright-line rule, and courts have been willing to find such duties where the substance of what a member actually did warranted it.

components.title: Does this LLP member owe a fiduciary duty?
components.description: A decision path for whether a duty arises absent an express LLP agreement term.

nodes.label: Does the LLP agreement (or a resolution under it) impose an express duty here?
Yes → the duty is contractual, defined by its terms
No → does the member perform a function involving discretion over the LLP's property or other members' interests (e.g. managing funds, negotiating on the LLP's behalf)?
Yes → a fiduciary duty may arise from that functional role (general agency/equity principles)
No → membership alone imposes no fiduciary duty; only the LLP Regulations 2001 default terms (if any) apply

components.textAlternative: First ask whether the LLP agreement imposes an express duty — if so, that duty is contractual and defined by its terms. If there is no agreement or it is silent, ask whether the member performs a function involving discretion over LLP property or other members' interests. If so, a fiduciary duty may arise from that functional role under general agency or equity principles. If not, membership alone imposes no fiduciary duty, and only the LLP Regulations 2001 default terms, if any apply, govern the relationship.

interaction.prompt: Put these sources of an LLP member's obligations in the order a solicitor should check them.
items: Check the LLP agreement for an express term
If silent, check whether the LLP Regulations 2001 default provisions cover the point
If still unresolved, consider whether the member's actual functional role attracts a fiduciary duty under general principles
Conclude only membership itself, with none of the above engaged, gives rise to no automatic duty
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the hierarchy: express agreement first, then the statutory default regulations, then general principles keyed to function — and only once all three are exhausted can you say membership alone creates no duty.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Reorder this by source of authority: contract (the LLP agreement) takes priority, then the Regulations' default terms, then general fiduciary principles tied to what the member actually does, and only last the conclusion that bare membership creates nothing.

parts.heading: Putting it together: a formation and duties scenario
parts.voice: case-narrative — applies the whole lesson to a single running client file
body: Two architects, Priya and Tomasz, want to set up an LLP. They file an incorporation document naming themselves as the only two members and stating both are designated members. The Registrar issues a certificate of incorporation dated 3 March.

Six months later, a former client discovers a defect in the original filing — the registered office address given was, in fact, one digit wrong. The former client argues the LLP was never validly incorporated and so cannot sue for unpaid fees. This argument fails: s 3's conclusive evidence rule means the certificate closes off exactly this kind of procedural challenge.

Separately, Tomasz starts handling all client funds and negotiating supplier contracts on the LLP's behalf, while Priya focuses on design work and takes no part in financial management. There is no LLP agreement. If Tomasz then diverts a supplier rebate into his own account, Priya's strongest argument is not 'LLP members automatically owe fiduciary duties' — it is that Tomasz's functional role, handling the LLP's money and negotiating on its behalf, is exactly the kind of discretion-bearing role that attracts a fiduciary duty under general principles, independent of any express agreement.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often answer that Priya can rely on 'the fiduciary duties LLP members owe each other' as if that were a settled, automatic legal rule, the way partners' duties under the Partnership Act 1890 are automatic.
components.whyItsWrong: LLP membership alone does not import that automatic regime. The stronger, legally accurate argument keys the duty to Tomasz's actual function — control over LLP funds and third-party negotiations — under general agency and equity principles, not to the bare fact that he is a member.

interaction.prompt: On the facts above, what is the legally soundest basis for arguing Tomasz owed a duty not to divert the supplier rebate?
options: LLP members automatically owe each other fiduciary duties in the same way traditional partners do
A fiduciary duty can arise from Tomasz's functional role handling LLP funds and negotiating supplier contracts, independent of any LLP agreement
No duty can arise at all in the absence of an express LLP agreement term covering financial management
interaction.explanation: Membership alone does not create an automatic fiduciary regime. But general principles can still impose a duty where a member's actual function — here, discretion over the LLP's money and dealings with third parties — is the kind of role equity has long treated as fiduciary.

testPool.prompt: A promoter wants to incorporate an LLP alone, planning to appoint a second member after the certificate is issued. Can the LLP be validly incorporated on this basis?
options: No — at least two persons must subscribe the incorporation document
Yes — the LLP can later add a second member to satisfy any minimum requirement
Yes — provided the sole promoter also names a designated member
No — but only because the promoter must also be a solicitor or accountant
testPool.explanation: LLPA 2000, s 2 requires at least two persons associated for carrying on a lawful business with a view to profit to subscribe the incorporation document. This cannot be cured retrospectively — the LLP simply cannot be incorporated on a single subscriber.

testPool.prompt: What does LLPA 2000, s 3 provide about the certificate of incorporation once issued?
options: It is conclusive evidence that the registration requirements of the Act have been complied with
It is rebuttable evidence, open to challenge if any procedural defect in registration is later found
It only takes effect once the LLP has traded for its first accounting period
It confirms the LLP's tax status but says nothing about its legal personality
testPool.explanation: Section 3 makes the certificate conclusive, not merely rebuttable, evidence of due incorporation — mirroring the equivalent provision for companies (CA 2006, s 15).

testPool.prompt: An LLP's incorporation document names two members but says nothing about designated members. Under s 8, what is the position?
options: No one is a designated member until a later notice specifies otherwise
The Registrar automatically appoints one member as sole designated member
Both members are treated as designated members by default
The LLP must re-file the incorporation document before it can trade
testPool.trapExplanation: It is tempting to think silence leaves a gap that needs fixing before the LLP can trade — but s 8(2) fills the gap automatically: where fewer than two designated members are named, every member becomes a designated member by default.
testPool.explanation: This default rule ensures there is never a period during which no one is responsible for the LLP's statutory filings.

testPool.prompt: Which statement best distinguishes an LLP member's exposure to the firm's debts from a general partner's exposure in a traditional partnership?
options: There is no difference — both are personally liable for all of the firm's debts without limit
An LLP member's liability on a winding up is capped at their agreed contribution, unlike a general partner's unlimited personal liability
An LLP member has no liability whatsoever, including on personal guarantees they have given
A general partner's liability is capped by statute in the same way an LLP member's is
testPool.trapExplanation: The trap is treating the LLP wrapper as blanket immunity — it protects a member from the firm's debts, but a personal guarantee given separately, or the member's own tortious liability, survives untouched.
testPool.explanation: Limited liability under the LLP structure caps exposure to the agreed contribution on a winding up; it does not erase separately assumed personal obligations.

testPool.prompt: A client asks what LLPA 2000, s 1 actually does, as distinct from the limited liability its members enjoy. What should the solicitor say?
options: Section 1 confers separate legal personality and unlimited capacity on the LLP as a body corporate; limited liability is a consequence of that separate personality, not a standalone grant
Section 1 is purely a tax provision and has no bearing on legal personality
Section 1 only applies once the LLP has appointed designated members
Section 1 limits members' liability directly, with separate legal personality arising from a different provision entirely
testPool.explanation: The structural move happens at s 1: making the LLP a body corporate separate from its members. Limited liability for members flows from that separate personality rather than being independently created.

testPool.prompt: Which of the following best describes the role the LLP Regulations 2001 play where an LLP has no LLP agreement?
options: They recreate, in full, the automatic fiduciary duties partners owe each other under the Partnership Act 1890
They supply a set of default provisions on matters like profit-sharing and management, without recreating a full automatic fiduciary regime
They prevent the LLP from trading until a formal agreement is put in place
They apply only to LLPs incorporated before 2001
testPool.explanation: The Regulations fill gaps left by a missing or incomplete LLP agreement with default terms, but they do not import the full fiduciary regime a traditional partnership carries automatically.

testPool.prompt: A former client argues an LLP was never validly formed because the registered office address on the incorporation document contained a typographical error, though a certificate of incorporation was later issued. Is the LLP's existence open to challenge on this basis?
options: No — the certificate of incorporation is conclusive evidence of due incorporation and forecloses this kind of procedural challenge
Yes — any error in the incorporation document, however minor, voids the certificate retrospectively
Yes, but only if the error was discovered within the LLP's first accounting period
No, but only because the former client lacks standing to raise the point at all
testPool.explanation: Section 3's conclusive evidence rule exists precisely to prevent this kind of collateral challenge to a completed incorporation based on a procedural defect in the filing.

testPool.prompt: An LLP member who gave a personal guarantee to the LLP's bank now argues the guarantee is unenforceable because LLP members enjoy limited liability. What should the solicitor advise?
options: The guarantee remains enforceable — limited liability protects a member from the LLP's debts, not from separately assumed personal obligations
The guarantee is automatically void once the LLP is incorporated, since limited liability overrides all prior personal commitments
The guarantee is enforceable only if the member was also a designated member at the time it was given
The guarantee is unenforceable unless it was referred to in the incorporation document
testPool.explanation: The LLP structure caps a member's exposure to the firm's own debts; it does not retrospectively unwind a personal guarantee that member separately chose to give.

testPool.prompt: A member with no management role and no LLP agreement in place is accused by a co-member of a breach of fiduciary duty simply for being a member who declined to disclose a personal business opportunity unrelated to the LLP. What is the solicitor's best initial advice?
options: Membership alone does not automatically impose fiduciary duties, so the accusation needs to identify some functional role or agreement term giving rise to a duty before it can succeed
The accusation must succeed, because all LLP members owe each other the same duties as partners under the Partnership Act 1890
The accusation must fail automatically, because LLP members can never owe fiduciary duties to one another under any circumstances
The outcome depends solely on whether the member in question was a designated member
testPool.explanation: The starting point is that bare membership creates no automatic fiduciary duty. Before advising the accusation has merit, the solicitor needs to find either an express agreement term or a functional role attracting a duty under general principles — neither of which is present on these facts.

testPool.prompt: One member of a two-member LLP takes on sole control of client money and all supplier negotiations, while the LLP agreement is silent on financial management. That member then diverts a supplier rebate to a personal account. What is the strongest legal basis for the other member's claim?
options: That LLP membership alone automatically imports the Partnership Act 1890 duties of good faith
That a fiduciary duty arose from the member's functional role controlling LLP funds and third-party negotiations, under general agency and equity principles
That the LLP Regulations 2001 create a criminal offence for diverting client money
That no claim is available because the LLP agreement did not expressly address financial management
testPool.explanation: Where a member takes on genuine control over the LLP's money and dealings with third parties, that functional role — not the bare fact of membership — is what can ground a fiduciary duty under general principles.

testPool.prompt: Which statement best summarises the designated members' statutory role under LLPA 2000, s 8?
options: They are responsible for the LLP's statutory filings, such as accounts and notifications of changes to the Registrar
They receive an automatically enhanced share of profits compared with ordinary members
They are the only members permitted to bind the LLP in contract with third parties
They must always be the LLP's most senior members by length of service
testPool.explanation: Designated member status is a compliance role, not a profit-share or seniority marker. It exists to fix responsibility for filings such as accounts and Registrar notifications.

testPool.prompt: An LLP incorporation document names three members but only one as a designated member. Which of the following correctly states the position under s 8?
options: The single named designated member alone bears the filing responsibilities
Because fewer than two designated members are named, all three members become designated members by default
The LLP is invalidly incorporated because it lacks a second designated member
The Registrar will reject the filing until a second designated member is nominated
testPool.trapExplanation: It's tempting to read a single named designated member as sufficient, but the statute requires at least two — naming only one has the same effect as naming none: the default rule applies and every member becomes designated.
testPool.explanation: Section 8(2) treats an incorporation document naming fewer than two designated members as if none were named, triggering the default position that every member is designated.

testPool.prompt: Does an LLP need to be formed for a charitable or non-profit purpose to qualify under the LLPA 2000?
options: No — the Act requires the members to be associated for carrying on a lawful business with a view to profit
Yes — non-profit purposes are the only lawful basis for LLP incorporation
No, but only registered charities may incorporate as LLPs
Yes, unless the LLP has fewer than five members
testPool.explanation: The statutory test is the reverse: incorporation requires a lawful business carried on with a view to profit, which is why the LLP structure is unsuited to non-profit ventures.

testPool.prompt: Which of the following best captures how a solicitor should describe LLP members' mutual duties in the absence of any LLP agreement?
options: Governed first by any applicable LLP Regulations 2001 default terms, with any further duty depending on the member's actual function rather than an automatic fiduciary regime
Identical in every respect to the fiduciary duties owed automatically between partners in a traditional partnership
Non-existent in all circumstances, since only an express LLP agreement can create obligations between members
Determined entirely by whichever member has been longest in the LLP
testPool.trapExplanation: The trap is assuming the LLP simply re-labels a traditional partnership — it does not. Without an agreement, the Regulations' defaults fill some gaps, and beyond that any duty depends on what the member actually does, not on membership itself.
testPool.explanation: This layered picture — agreement, then Regulations, then function-based general principles — is the accurate account rather than treating either extreme (full automatic duties, or none at all) as correct.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The recurring mistake in this lesson is importing the traditional partnership's automatic fiduciary regime wholesale into the LLP context. Check first for an agreement term, then the Regulations' defaults, then whether the member's actual function — not their membership — attracts a duty.
